meta.subject: Number Theory
meta.demo_path_note: Walkable in order: every node's prereqs appear before it. bases, bezout and linear_diophantine were added on 2026-08-19 because the original 16-node path reached mod_exp, mod_inverse and linear_congruence before their prerequisites. graph.py validate() enforces this.
meta.notes: Tiers 0-1 are the demo surface. Tiers 2-3 exist so the graph has depth to show, but do not author problems for them unless there is time left over.

tiers.name: Core foundation
tiers.desc: Arithmetic structure of the integers. No modular language yet.

tiers.name: Contest foundation
tiers.desc: Modular arithmetic and the classical theorems. This is where most contest number theory lives.

tiers.name: Olympiad
tiers.desc: Valuations, quadratic residues, multiplicative machinery, descent.

tiers.name: Applied / computational
tiers.desc: Algorithms and cryptography built on tier 1.

nodes.name: Divisibility and multiples
nodes.concept: a | b means b = ak for some integer k. Divisibility is transitive and respects integer linear combinations.
nodes.assesses: Can the student decide whether one integer divides another and chain divisibility facts?
nodes.generator: Given random a in [2,20], k in [2,30], b = a*k (+ optional offset r != 0 for negative cases): 'Does a divide b?' or 'Find all divisors of b under 50.' Answer computed directly.

nodes.name: Primes and composites
nodes.concept: A prime has exactly two positive divisors. Trial division up to sqrt(n) is sufficient to test primality.
nodes.assesses: Can the student classify n and justify stopping trial division at sqrt(n)?
nodes.generator: Random n in [50,400], biased 50/50 prime vs semiprime. Ask 'is n prime' or 'what is the largest prime you must test'.

nodes.name: Prime factorization
nodes.concept: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer > 1 has a unique multiset of prime factors.
nodes.assesses: Can the student produce the canonical factorization and read exponents off it?
nodes.generator: Sample 2-4 primes from [2,17] with exponents 1-3, multiply to get n. Ask for the factorization or for a specific prime's exponent.

nodes.name: GCD and LCM
nodes.concept: gcd takes min exponents, lcm takes max exponents, and gcd(a,b) * lcm(a,b) = ab.
nodes.assesses: Can the student compute both from factorizations and use the product identity?
nodes.generator: Build a and b from a shared prime pool so the gcd is non-trivial. Ask for gcd, lcm, or the missing value given the other three in the identity.

nodes.name: Euclidean algorithm
nodes.concept: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b). Terminates because the remainder strictly decreases.
nodes.assesses: Can the student run the algorithm on numbers too large to factor by hand?
nodes.generator: a, b random in [10^3, 10^5] with a controlled gcd. Ask for gcd, or for the number of division steps.
nodes.verify: sympy.gcd; step count from a reference implementation

nodes.name: Divisor count and sum
nodes.concept: For n = prod p_i^e_i, tau(n) = prod (e_i + 1) and sigma(n) = prod (p_i^(e_i+1) - 1)/(p_i - 1).
nodes.assesses: Can the student go from factorization to divisor statistics without listing divisors?
nodes.generator: Same construction as factorization. Ask for tau(n), sigma(n), or 'find the smallest n with exactly k divisors'.

nodes.name: Base representation
nodes.concept: Every n has a unique representation in base b as a sum of digits times powers of b.
nodes.assesses: Can the student convert both directions and reason about digit counts?
nodes.generator: Random n in [100, 5000], base in {2,3,5,7,8,16}. Convert, or ask for digit count / leading digit.

nodes.name: Digit sums and divisibility rules
nodes.concept: Divisibility rules for 3, 9, 11 come from 10 ≡ 1 (mod 3, 9) and 10 ≡ -1 (mod 11).
nodes.assesses: Can the student apply a rule and, more importantly, explain why it works?
nodes.generator: Construct an n-digit number with one digit left as an unknown; ask for the digit making it divisible by 3, 9, or 11.
nodes.verify: modular check over all 10 digit values

nodes.name: Congruence relation
nodes.concept: a ≡ b (mod n) iff n | (a - b). It is an equivalence relation and partitions Z into residue classes.
nodes.assesses: Can the student translate between the divisibility and congruence statements?
nodes.generator: Random n in [3,30], a in [0,500]. Ask for the residue, or whether two given numbers are congruent.

nodes.name: Modular addition and multiplication
nodes.concept: Congruence is preserved under addition, subtraction, and multiplication, but not division.
nodes.assesses: Can the student reduce early instead of computing the full product?
nodes.generator: Random large a, b and modulus n. Ask for (a*b + c) mod n. Include one distractor per set where naive division fails.

nodes.name: Modular exponentiation
nodes.concept: Repeated squaring computes a^k mod n in O(log k) multiplications using the binary expansion of k.
nodes.assesses: Can the student compute a^k mod n for k far beyond brute force?
nodes.generator: a in [2,50], k in [10^3, 10^6], n in [7, 200]. Ask for the value, or for the last digit of a^k.

nodes.name: Modular inverses
nodes.concept: a has an inverse mod n iff gcd(a,n) = 1; the extended Euclidean algorithm constructs it.
nodes.assesses: Can the student decide existence and then construct the inverse?
nodes.generator: Pick n, then a coprime to n half the time and sharing a factor the other half. Ask for the inverse or 'explain why none exists'.

nodes.name: Bezout's identity
nodes.concept: There exist integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a,b), found by back-substituting the Euclidean algorithm.
nodes.assesses: Can the student run extended Euclid and produce a valid (x,y)?
nodes.generator: a, b in [10, 500]. Ask for any valid pair; the grader accepts any (x,y) satisfying the equation, not one canonical answer.

nodes.name: Linear Diophantine equations
nodes.concept: ax + by = c has integer solutions iff gcd(a,b) | c, and then infinitely many in an arithmetic family.
nodes.assesses: Can the student decide solvability and describe the full solution family?
nodes.generator: Choose a, b, then c as either a multiple of gcd (solvable) or not (unsolvable). Ask for a solution or the smallest positive x.

nodes.name: Linear congruences
nodes.concept: ax ≡ b (mod n) has gcd(a,n) solutions mod n when gcd(a,n) | b, and none otherwise.
nodes.assesses: Can the student count solutions, not just find one?
nodes.generator: Vary gcd(a,n) across 1, 2, and a non-dividing case. Ask for all solutions mod n.
nodes.verify: brute-force residue scan on the reference side

nodes.name: Chinese remainder theorem
nodes.concept: Pairwise coprime moduli give a unique solution modulo their product.
nodes.assesses: Can the student combine systems, and recognize when moduli are not coprime?
nodes.generator: 2-3 congruences with coprime moduli from {3,4,5,7,9,11}. Occasionally emit a non-coprime consistent/inconsistent pair as a trap.

nodes.name: Fermat's little theorem
nodes.concept: For prime p and gcd(a,p)=1, a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Reduces exponents mod p-1.
nodes.assesses: Can the student reduce a huge exponent using the theorem rather than by squaring?
nodes.generator: Prime p in [7,97], a coprime to p, exponent k in [10^4, 10^9]. Ask for a^k mod p.

nodes.name: Euler's totient function
nodes.concept: phi(n) counts integers in [1,n] coprime to n; phi is multiplicative and phi(p^e) = p^e - p^(e-1).
nodes.assesses: Can the student compute phi from a factorization and use multiplicativity?
nodes.generator: n built from 2-3 primes with exponents. Ask for phi(n), or for n given phi(n) in small cases.

nodes.name: Euler's theorem
nodes.concept: a^phi(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) when gcd(a,n)=1. Generalizes Fermat to composite moduli.
nodes.assesses: Can the student reduce exponents mod phi(n) for composite n?
nodes.generator: Composite n in [15,200], a coprime to n, exponent k large. Ask for a^k mod n.

nodes.name: Multiplicative order and cyclicity
nodes.concept: The order of a mod n is the least k > 0 with a^k ≡ 1, and it always divides phi(n).
nodes.assesses: Can the student find the order by testing divisors of phi(n) rather than all k?
nodes.generator: n and coprime a. Ask for ord_n(a), or for the cycle length of the last digits of a^k.

nodes.name: Wilson's theorem
nodes.concept: (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) exactly when p is prime.
nodes.assesses: Can the student use factorial congruences and the primality characterization?
nodes.generator: Prime or composite p in [5,40]. Ask for (p-1)! mod p.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole in number theory
nodes.concept: Among n+1 integers, two share a residue mod n, the standard route to 'some subset is divisible by n' claims.
nodes.assesses: Can the student spot when a residue-class counting argument closes a problem?
nodes.generator: Hard to auto-generate. Hand-author 3-5 problems; keep this node proof-flavoured and mark it non-generated.

nodes.name: p-adic valuation
nodes.concept: v_p(n) is the exponent of p in n; v_p(ab) = v_p(a) + v_p(b).

nodes.name: Legendre's formula
nodes.concept: v_p(n!) = sum floor(n / p^i); counts trailing zeros and factorial divisibility.

nodes.name: Lifting the exponent
nodes.concept: v_p(a^n - b^n) decomposes cleanly when p | a - b; the workhorse for exponential divisibility.

nodes.name: Quadratic residues
nodes.concept: Exactly half the nonzero residues mod an odd prime are squares; Euler's criterion tests membership.

nodes.name: Legendre symbol and reciprocity
nodes.concept: Quadratic reciprocity relates (p|q) and (q|p), turning residue tests into a fast algorithm.

nodes.name: Primitive roots
nodes.concept: A primitive root generates the whole multiplicative group; they exist exactly for n = 1,2,4,p^k,2p^k.

nodes.name: Multiplicative functions and Mobius
nodes.concept: Dirichlet convolution of multiplicative functions is multiplicative; mu is the inverse of the constant function 1.

nodes.name: Mobius inversion
nodes.concept: Recovers f from its divisor-sum, the standard tool for counting-by-divisor problems.

nodes.name: Infinite descent and Vieta jumping
nodes.concept: Assume a minimal solution, construct a smaller one, contradiction. The core olympiad Diophantine technique.

nodes.name: Sum of two squares
nodes.concept: n is a sum of two squares iff every prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) appears to an even power.

nodes.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
nodes.concept: Mark composites by stepping through multiples; O(n log log n) primes up to n.

nodes.name: Probabilistic primality testing
nodes.concept: Fermat and Miller-Rabin tests, plus why Carmichael numbers defeat the naive version.

nodes.name: RSA
nodes.concept: Key generation from two large primes; encryption and decryption are inverse exponentiations mod n.
